title: I built a full idle kingdom builder with an AI coding agent – here's what worked and what needed a simulation bot
author: Original-Fall6524
selftext:
Game (free, browser, no account): https://mahishmati-delta.vercel.app

Mahishmati is a single-player idle kingdom builder set in an original Indian epic-fantasy world: economy, staffing and housing, a tech tree, five unit types with matchups, territories to conquer, an advisor court and a prestige layer.

How it was built: I used Claude Code as the main developer. It's React and TypeScript with a pure simulation engine (no DOM or timers inside), so every rule is unit-tested with injected time and seeded randomness. All art is procedural SVG written as code, so there are no AI image generators involved. Sound is synthesized with Web Audio.

What helped most: a balance bot that plays the game for 1.5 hours in tests (and 6 hours in a longer run) and prints a timeline. It caught pacing problems that reading the formulas never would. Battle odds come from an exact grid over both random rolls, so the number shown matches what actually happens.

What I'd like from you:
- If you've used agents for game balance, did you trust bot playthroughs, or did they miss what humans notice?
- Play 10 minutes: does it feel hand-tuned or generated?

comments.author: Noah__1302
comments.body: Did the bot’s timeline catch pacing problems that you later confirmed with humans, or did it flag things that felt fine to players? I’m asking because I’m doing the same thing with a bot for an incremental game, and the “dry streak” metric (runs in a row with nothing affordable) has been the most useful output so far.

replies.author: Original-Fall6524
replies.body:
Honest answer: not confirmed with humans yet. It only just went out, so threads like this are the human check.

The bot plays greedy "perfect" play: taps for the first 10 minutes, builds the cheapest useful option, researches whenever it can afford to, and only attacks at 85%+ odds. The test asserts guard-rails rather than feel: the tutorial completes, no NaN/Infinity anywhere, the fort that unlocks the next era falls between 30 and 90 minutes, and at least 10 techs are known by 1.5 hours.

Where it earned its keep was the shape of the timeline: after a number change, a milestone sliding out of its window shows up immediately. What it can't tell me is how much slower a human is early on, or whether a wait *feels* boring, because it never hesitates.

Your dry-streak metric is a really good idea. "There's always something to build, research or decide" is a design rule for this game, and I don't measure it directly yet. Do you count a stretch as dry when nothing at all is affordable, or when nothing *useful* is?

replies.author: Noah__1302
replies.body: Fair point, and “nothing useful” is a better definition than mine. My dry streak only counts runs where nothing at all was affordable. Your point that the bot never hesitates is the one I keep coming back to. How do you define “useful” for your game: by the milestone you’re pacing toward, or by whether a purchase changes the next 10 minutes?

replies.author: Original-Fall6524
replies.body:
Honestly, neither yet, and it's cruder than either of your options. Survival rules run first (build a farm if net food is about to go negative, a house if housing is nearly full, storage when a resource is near its cap). After that the bot buys whatever affordable building has the lowest weighted cost, with a 1.3x discount for anything that produces or raises army cap. So "useful" is really "cheap and productive", with no look-ahead.

Your second option is the one I'd move to: count a purchase as useful if it shortens the time to the next milestone (next territory, next tech) by more than some threshold. That would also give me a proper dry-streak signal: stretches where nothing affordable moves the next milestone closer, even though there's technically something to buy. Thanks, this is a better metric than the one I have.

comments.author: Jin_Sakai_Ghost
comments.body:
Umm... Feels slop.

There might have been some thought process behind it all, but what turned out feels like just a random set of things pit together haphazardly just for the sake of creating a game.

replies.author: Original-Fall6524
replies.body:
Fair hit, and thanks for saying it straight. I can see how it reads as a pile of systems rather than one idea.

What felt most random to you: the buildings and resources themselves, the events that pop up, or how they connect (or don't)? I'd rather cut things than keep stacking, so knowing which part felt bolted on helps a lot.

replies.author: Jin_Sakai_Ghost
replies.body:
Honestly, there is too much reading, and it wasn't actually fun or engaging for me.

It felt like a chore, just doing things for the sake of doing things, with no end goal or outcome to target.
